focusPost.content: It’s ironic how we blame China for our own manufacturing inferiority. As the article states, “Chinese manufacturers are adept at mass-producing electric vehicles.” The problem is ours, not theirs. It’s simply a reflection of our money obsessed culture that prizes profits above all else. Above health. More than life itself. Our laws and court actions have repeatedly reaffirmed a company’s highest responsibility is to “maximize shareholder value.” Which means make as much money as possible, as quickly as possible, any way possible. The fastest way a manufacturing company can boost its profits is to cut costs. Mortgage the future for the sake of a few more dollars today. In the process we’ve ceded manufacturing to China and other countries who can make EVs, and most other manufactured goods, better than we can. Over the past few decades we’ve rationalized becoming a “service” economy or an “information” economy. Funny how making things is still important. Cars, iPhones, solar panels, wind turbines, batteries, all of which we rely on China to make for us. By resorting to tariffs we’re only making consumers pay more for things that we can’t manufacture as well or as inexpensively as others can. If we want to blame someone for our loss of manufacturing prowess, we have only to look in the mirror.

I don't see the problem with letting China pump and dump, at massive losses, cars from their EV industry. What better way to fund the energy transition, which will make us less dependent on Russia and other rouge dictatorships, than with Chinese govt money? 

Just cut red tape on US lithium mining and subsidize/tariff protect our own industries just enough that the companies continue to grow it capture the luxury market, then let China pay for the masses to convert to EVs and solar. It would be very easy; just do economic analysis on which EV types China sells at a loss, allow those in, then tariff the big and luxury ones that turn a profit. They're desperate to sell bc they already made the capex investments on the factories, so we can dictate terms

Complain all you want about Chinese auto starting to dominate, but if EV is the key to fighting climate change, than shutting Chinese auto out of a car-crazed US market seems like another side of the"climate -denial" coin.  Not to mention a slap in the face of Americans under the thumb of inflation. 

I agree with the concern of Chinese spyware in American roads, but I also have concerned GM and Ford and Tesla spyware too.  So fix the problem if automotive spyware, and let me buy a half-wat decent inexpensive Chinese EV. 

...Because I ain't buying a bloated, expensive American EV.

In the U.S., we value clean air and clean water, and support a level of environmental respect for the planet.  Not as much as we should, but more than what those in China live with.  That costs money. In an ironic twist of fate, that’s one factor that keeps the fossil fuel based cars on the road here,  in place of renewable energy EVs filling the roads in China.  ( obviously, the cleaner only refers to the operation and not manufacturing). Furthermore, workers building cars in North America earn more making the cars that are much pricier, and the flood of cheaper Chinese cars would undermine the ability of American workers to buy these or any cars. In America, our environmental values, our economy, are just not ready to compete with the global marketplace we created.  It’s been obvious to the American worker, and the American consumer for decades now. While we hoped globalization would bring equality to the world, we also hoped that would happen by raising standards across the globe.  What really has happened, and to everyone but the few richest people,  is the opposite.  We became ‘more equal’ by lowering expectations, opportunities, and real economic security here at home. These cars, perhaps more than any other product that China has mass produced, reflect that reality.

For 20 years I’ve been hearing how important it is that we shift away from the internal combustion engine. Now, the Chinese have affordable electric vehicles while American and European companies continue selling expensive gas-powered cars. And instead of letting the free market take its course, the hegemonic powers of the west argue about Chinese overcapacity and government subsidies. 

This is how the US and Europe lose their positions as world leaders. They are too busy protecting entrenched interests to truly do something about the environment and to give consumers the options they want. And developing countries are the first ones to witness it. I live in Mexico and I can tell you that we have a bunch of new Chinese cars on the roads. Americans and Europeans won’t see this because they are shielded by tariffs, but you cannot change global economic dynamics with simple domestic policies.

A major credit to Chinese automakers, they understand the need for mass produced affordable EVs for the consumer market and have made huge amount of progress. Whereas in the US, a mass produced affordable EV is still a dream. EVs here are exorbitantly priced luxury items and the factors driving that are mostly corporate greed. Wall street loves the huge margins from EV sales and so do the EV makers, there is presently no incentive for any of the players here to cater for that need. Instead of competing with Chinese EVs, we effectively close the market to them by putting tariffs. Why should we grudge Chinese success in this aspect when we do not do anything to compete for that particular market segment?

Copying and making it better and cheaper. The Chinese automakers have beaten the US automakers at their own game. With State sponsorship. 

Copying anyone is the best compliment anyone can pay.

The US has to learn manufacturing anew with new technologies. Quality products at scale which are economical to produce for domestic consumption and exports. Beat the competition at their own game. Are we ready?

Tariffs and protectionism take us backwards. 

Otherwise, the whole world will pass us by in autonomous electric vehicles on the road and in the sky and we will still be stuck in the ICE age! Driving noisy gas guzzlers polluting our own air!

So if the majority if not all of the parts used in American autos are manufactured in China are not they Chinese cars too?  

Even if they are assembled in the USA or Mexico?

I went to the company web site.  OEM.
The part was made in China.

I then went to the aftermarket brands, and all of them were made in China or with Chinese parts in mexico.

I then checked the rebuilt shop for a used reconditioned starter, but all the internal replacment parts were made in China.

Even the other imports from other countries are made with Chinese part.  VW is moving production to China.

So directly or indirectly, we are all driving Chinese cars in the United States already.

If we want to blame someone for our loss of manufacturing prowess, we have only to look in the mirror.

For decades the US was the champion and extolled the virtues of free market capitalism and free trade. The greatest and surest way for growth and prosperity.

Now, when the US faces competition which it cannot win with the rules it crafted, it’s crying foul.

Copying and making it better and cheaper. The Chinese automakers have beaten the US automakers at their own game. With State sponsorship. 

Copying anyone is the best compliment anyone can pay.

The US has to learn manufacturing anew with new technologies. Quality products at scale which are economical to produce for domestic consumption and exports. Beat the competition at their own game. Are we ready?

Tariffs and protectionism take us backwards. 

Otherwise, the whole world will pass us by in autonomous electric vehicles on the road and in the sky and we will still be stuck in the ICE age! Driving noisy gas guzzlers polluting our own air!

A major credit to Chinese automakers, they understand the need for mass produced affordable EVs for the consumer market and have made huge amount of progress. Whereas in the US, a mass produced affordable EV is still a dream. EVs here are exorbitantly priced luxury items and the factors driving that are mostly corporate greed. Wall street loves the huge margins from EV sales and so do the EV makers, there is presently no incentive for any of the players here to cater for that need. Instead of competing with Chinese EVs, we effectively close the market to them by putting tariffs. Why should we grudge Chinese success in this aspect when we do not do anything to compete for that particular market segment?

nothing encapsulates absurdity better than antagonistic policy positions

In my country anyway, Government policy explicitly punishes combustion engine owners and rewards electric vehicle owners. Through taxation, subsidy, lack of environmental accountability on manufacturing and constant messaging about how massive changes are necessary in lifestyles. Every natural event is somehow framed as a result of profligacy and neglect on the part of the citizenry. God is angry, essentially.

I am told constantly that I must change my ways. I need a new electric vehicle. Now, I am old enough to know that when the weather forecaster is selling umbrellas, something ain't right.
So, apparently what needs to happen is for me to buy a Ford electric vehicle. Lots of advertising for those. But those ads are on the same websites telling me that this is an emergency. An existential crisis. The most important thing. 

And yet the same Government won't allow inexpensive EVs to be sold here. So forgive me if I take all of this doom as a sales maneuver. 

You could allow Chinese EVs, and ban cryptocurrency mining, and solve electricity supply. But that's actually not what anyone wants. Governments want to fund projects, and sell specific new vehicles from favoured manufacturers. And endless crisis generation/management is simply an over the top way to keep this going.

I don't get it

In the US, 
1. Ford loses 1.5 billion making EVs and each one is 50k or more
2. GM is slow walking EV (they made less than 1000) 
3. Tesla will be out of business if not for the energy credits given  generously by the US govt
4. There is no sales tax in many states on "domestic" EVs, a state subsidy! 
5. Federal govt is giving $7500 for buying an EV, a federal subsidy!

And the Chinese are flooding the global market with cheap EVs!

Go figure!

Complain all you want about Chinese auto starting to dominate, but if EV is the key to fighting climate change, than shutting Chinese auto out of a car-crazed US market seems like another side of the"climate -denial" coin.  Not to mention a slap in the face of Americans under the thumb of inflation. 

I agree with the concern of Chinese spyware in American roads, but I also have concerned GM and Ford and Tesla spyware too.  So fix the problem if automotive spyware, and let me buy a half-wat decent inexpensive Chinese EV. 

...Because I ain't buying a bloated, expensive American EV.
What happened to American ingenuity in making great cars that all Americans can afford? Henry Ford must be spinning in his grave that Made in the USA can't compete with China when it comes to EVs.

For 20 years I’ve been hearing how important it is that we shift away from the internal combustion engine. Now, the Chinese have affordable electric vehicles while American and European companies continue selling expensive gas-powered cars. And instead of letting the free market take its course, the hegemonic powers of the west argue about Chinese overcapacity and government subsidies. 

This is how the US and Europe lose their positions as world leaders. They are too busy protecting entrenched interests to truly do something about the environment and to give consumers the options they want. And developing countries are the first ones to witness it. I live in Mexico and I can tell you that we have a bunch of new Chinese cars on the roads. Americans and Europeans won’t see this because they are shielded by tariffs, but you cannot change global economic dynamics with simple domestic policies.
